questions.title: GATE CSE 2001 | Question: 1.3
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Consider two well-formed formulas in propositional logic

$F_1: P \Rightarrow \neg P$          $F_2: (P \Rightarrow \neg P) \lor ( \neg P \Rightarrow P)$

Which one of the following statements is correct?

  1. $F_1$ is satisfiable, $F_2$ is valid
  2. $F_1$ unsatisfiable, $F_2$ is satisfiable
  3. $F_1$ is unsatisfiable, $F_2$ is valid
  4. $F_1$ and $F_2$ are both satisfiable

review.independentCheck: F1 is equivalent to not P and is satisfiable; F2 simplifies to not P or P, a tautology.
review.notes: F1 is equivalent to not P and is satisfiable; F2 simplifies to not P or P, a tautology.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2001 | Question: 2.1
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
How many $4$-digit even numbers have all $4$ digits distinct?

  1. $2240$
  2. $2296$
  3. $2620$
  4. $4536$

review.independentCheck: Count separately for final digit 0 and for one of 2,4,6,8: 504+1792=2296.
review.notes: Count separately for final digit 0 and for one of 2,4,6,8: 504+1792=2296.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2001 | Question: 2.2
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following statements:

  • $S_1:$ There exists infinite sets $A$, $B$, $C$ such that $A \cap (B \cup C)$ is finite.
  • $S_2:$ There exists two irrational numbers $x$ and y such that $(x+y)$ is rational.

Which of the following is true about $S_1$ and $S_2$?

  1. Only $S_1$ is correct
  2. Only $S_2$ is correct
  3. Both $S_1$ and $S_2$ are correct
  4. None of $S_1$ and $S_2$ is correct

review.independentCheck: Disjoint infinite even/odd sets witness S1; sqrt(2) and -sqrt(2) witness S2.
review.notes: Disjoint infinite even/odd sets witness S1; sqrt(2) and -sqrt(2) witness S2.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2001 | Question: 2.3
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $f: A \rightarrow B$ a function, and let E and F be subsets of $A$. Consider the following statements about images.

  • $S_1: f(E \cup F) = f(E) \cup f(F)$
  • $S_2: f(E \cap F)=f(E) \cap f(F)$

Which of the following is true about S1 and S2?

  1. Only $S_1$ is correct
  2. Only $S_2$ is correct
  3. Both $S_1$ and $S_2$ are correct
  4. None of $S_1$ and $S_2$ is correct

review.independentCheck: Images distribute over unions; a constant function on disjoint singleton sets disproves intersection equality.
review.notes: Images distribute over unions; a constant function on disjoint singleton sets disproves intersection equality.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2001 | Question: 2.4
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Seven (distinct) car accidents occurred in a week. What is the probability that they all occurred on the same day?

  2. $\dfrac{1}{7^6}\\$
  3. $\dfrac{1}{2^7}\\$
  4. $\dfrac{7}{2^7}\\$

review.independentCheck: Seven favorable common-day assignments among 7^7 total assignments give 1/7^6.
review.notes: Seven favorable common-day assignments among 7^7 total assignments give 1/7^6.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2001 | Question: 2.15
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.1
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
X, Y and Z are closed intervals of unit length on the real line. The overlap of X and Y is half a unit. The overlap of Y and Z is also half a unit. Let the overlap of X and Z be k units. Which of the following is true?

  1. k must be 1
  2. k must be 0
  3. k can take any value between 0 and 1
  4. None of the above

review.independentCheck: For unit intervals, the two half-unit overlaps force each adjacent pair of left endpoints to differ by 1/2. Consequently the X-Z overlap can only be 0 or 1, not an arbitrary intermediate value such as 1/2. The existing key and GateOverflow page mark option C ('can take any value between 0 and 1'), which conflicts with the literal wording; retain on HOLD pending a source/wording resolution.
review.notes: For unit intervals, the two half-unit overlaps force each adjacent pair of left endpoints to differ by 1/2. Consequently the X-Z overlap can only be 0 or 1, not an arbitrary intermediate value such as 1/2. The existing key and GateOverflow page mark option C ('can take any value between 0 and 1'), which conflicts with the literal wording; retain on HOLD pending a source/wording resolution.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record and GateOverflow question page; an unresolved wording/answer conflict remains.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.2
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
$E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$  are events in a probability space satisfying the following constraints:

  • $Pr$$\left ( E_{1} \right )$ = $Pr$$\left ( E_{2} \right )$
  • $Pr$$\left ( E_{1}\cup E_{2} \right )$ = $1$
  • $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ are independent

The value of $Pr$$\left ( E_{1} \right )$, the probability of the event $E_{1}$,  is

  1.  $0$
  2. $\dfrac{1}{4}$
  3. $\dfrac{1}{2}$
  4.  $1$

review.independentCheck: The union equation reduces to 1=2p-p^2, so p=1.
review.notes: The union equation reduces to 1=2p-p^2, so p=1.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.3
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $S = \sum_{i=3}^{100} i \log_{2} i$, and $T = \int_{2}^{100} x \log_{2}x dx$.

Which of the following statements is true?

  1. $S > T$
  2. $S = T$
  3. $S < T$ and $2S > T$
  4. $2S ≤ T$

review.independentCheck: x log2(x) is strictly increasing for x>=2; compare each integral interval [i-1,i] with its right endpoint term.
review.notes: x log2(x) is strictly increasing for x>=2; compare each integral interval [i-1,i] with its right endpoint term.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.4
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
A polynomial $p(x)$ satisfies the following:

  • $p(1) = p(3) = p(5) = 1$ 
  • $p(2) = p(4) = -1$

The minimum degree of such a polynomial is

  1. $1$
  2. $2$
  3. $3$
  4. $4$

review.independentCheck: Five-point interpolation permits degree four; nonzero fourth forward difference rules out degree at most three.
review.notes: Five-point interpolation permits degree four; nonzero fourth forward difference rules out degree at most three.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.5
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
A relation $R$ is defined on the set of integers as $xRy$ iff $(x + y)$ is even. Which of the following statements is true?

  1. $R$ is not an equivalence relation
  2. $R$ is an equivalence relation having $1$ equivalence class
  3. $R$ is an equivalence relation having $2$ equivalence classes
  4. $R$ is an equivalence relation having $3$ equivalence classes

review.independentCheck: The relation is equality of parity and has the even and odd classes.
review.notes: The relation is equality of parity and has the even and odd classes.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.6
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $P(S)$ denotes the power set of set $S.$ Which of the following is always true?

  1. $P(P(S)) = P(S)$
  2. $P(S) ∩ P(P(S)) = \{ Ø \}$
  3. $P(S) ∩ S = P(S)$
  4. $S ∉ P(S)$

review.independentCheck: With arbitrary sets in standard set theory, option B is not always true: for S={empty set}, P(S) intersect P(P(S)) contains both empty set and {empty set}. The existing answer record and GateOverflow key mark B, relying on an unstated restriction on the elements of S. Since the stem says 'always', retain on HOLD rather than asserting the restricted interpretation.
review.notes: With arbitrary sets in standard set theory, option B is not always true: for S={empty set}, P(S) intersect P(P(S)) contains both empty set and {empty set}. The existing answer record and GateOverflow key mark B, relying on an unstated restriction on the elements of S. Since the stem says 'always', retain on HOLD rather than asserting the restricted interpretation.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.7
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $a, b, c, d$ be propositions. Assume that the equivalence $a ⇔ ( b \vee \neg b)$ and $b ⇔c$ hold. Then the truth-value of the formula $(a ∧ b) → (a ∧ c) ∨ d$ is always

  1. True
  2. False
  3. Same as the truth-value of $b$
  4. Same as the truth-value of $d$

review.independentCheck: a is true and b=c; if b is true the consequent is true, otherwise the antecedent is false.
review.notes: a is true and b=c; if b is true the consequent is true, otherwise the antecedent is false.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.1
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose that the expectation of a random variable $X$ is $5$. Which of the following statements is true?

  1. There is a sample point at which $X$ has the value $5$.
  2. There is a sample point at which $X$ has value greater than $5$.
  3. There is a sample point at which $X$ has a value greater than equal to $5$.
  4. None of the above.

review.independentCheck: If all X values were below five then their expectation would be below five; thus some value is at least five.
review.notes: If all X values were below five then their expectation would be below five; thus some value is at least five.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.1
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Consider two events $E_1$ and $E_2$ such that probability of $E_1$, $P_r[E_1]=\frac{1}{2}$, probability of $E_2$, $P_r[E_{2}]=\frac{1}{3}$, and probability of $E_1$, and $E_2$, $P_r[E_1 \: and \: E_2] = \frac{1}{5}$. Which of the following statements is/are true?

  1. $P_r[E_1\: \text{or} \:E_2] \text{ is } \frac{2}{3}$

  2. Events $E_1$ and $E_2$ are independent

  3. Events $E_1$ and $E_2$ are not independent

  4. $P_r \left[{E_1}\mid{E_2} \right] = \frac{4}{5}$

review.independentCheck: A binary relation is a subset of A cross A, so there are 2^(n^2).
review.notes: A binary relation is a subset of A cross A, so there are 2^(n^2).

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 2.3
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $L$ be a set with a relation $R$ which is transitive, anti-symmetric and reflexive and for any two elements $a, b \in  L$, let the least upper bound $lub (a, b)$ and the greatest lower bound $glb (a, b)$ exist. Which of the following is/are true?

  1. $L$ is a poset

  2. $L$ is a Boolean algebra

  3. $L$ is a lattice

  4. None of the above

review.independentCheck: The axioms define a poset and pairwise lub/glb make it a lattice; Boolean structure is not implied.
